facts.title: Visa-free for up to 90 days
facts.body: No visa needed with a Dutch passport for up to 90 days. The passport must be valid for the whole stay.

facts.title: Visit Japan Web
facts.body: Optional but recommended: one QR code for immigration and customs. Save a screenshot; paper forms still work.

facts.title: Red zone in south-east Fukushima
facts.body: The nuclear exclusion area (towns such as Futaba, Iitate, Katsurao, Minamisōma, Namie, Okuma and Tomioka) is red: do not go. The rest of Japan is green.

facts.title: Drink spiking in nightlife areas
facts.body: Occasionally in Roppongi, Shibuya, Shinjuku and Kabukicho (Tokyo) or Namba (Osaka). Keep your drink in sight; accept nothing from strangers.

facts.title: Earthquakes and tsunamis
facts.body: High chance of earthquakes, landslides and tsunamis. Install an alert app (see Useful apps).

facts.title: Typhoons
facts.body: Tropical storms and typhoons occur; follow local news and the Japan Meteorological Agency when one is forecast.

facts.title: Japan Visitor Hotline (JNTO), 24/7
facts.body: 050-3816-2787 (+81 50 3816 2787 from abroad): tourist information and help with accidents, illness and disasters, in English, Chinese and Korean.

facts.title: Slow consular notice after arrest
facts.body: If you are arrested it can take a long time before the Dutch embassy is told.

facts.title: Drugs
facts.body: Heavy fines and long prison sentences for using, possessing or selling drugs.

facts.title: Tattoos
facts.body: Tattoos are associated with gangs; some pools, onsen, spas and gyms refuse entry. Look for tattoo-friendly places.

facts.title: E-liquid: 120 ml per month
facts.body: Maximum 120 ml of e-cigarette liquid per month for personal use; more risks a fine or prison. It isn't sold in Japan.

facts.title: Medicines: one-month rule
facts.body: Up to one month's supply of ordinary prescription medicine (two months over-the-counter) without paperwork; more needs an Import Confirmation (Yunyu Kakunin-sho) applied for online before arrival. Amphetamine-type ADHD medicine is prohibited; some substances (e.g. pseudoephedrine) are controlled. Keep medicines in the original packaging.

sources.title: Bringing medicines for personal use into Japan — MHLW

facts.title: Expensive care, limited English
facts.body: Treatment and hospital stays can cost more than in the Netherlands, and staff speak less English. Good travel insurance matters.

facts.title: Carry cash
facts.body: Cards (credit or debit) aren't accepted everywhere — always carry enough cash.

facts.title: Tax-free shopping becomes a refund (from 1 Nov 2026)
facts.body: From 1 November 2026 tax-free shops charge the full price including tax; you claim the tax back when you leave Japan, before checking in, at a customs terminal at the airport. Show your passport when buying; export the goods within 90 days. Items used up in Japan don't qualify.

sources.title: Changes are coming to Japan's tax-free shopping — JNTO

facts.title: IC card: Welcome Suica
facts.body: Welcome Suica (card, or the Welcome Suica Mobile app on iPhone) is prepaid e-money for trains, buses and shops. The app can also hold JR East seat reservations. Some features only work once you are in Japan.

facts.title: Driving needs an IDP (1949 model)
facts.body: A Dutch licence is only valid together with an IDP of the 1949 model, from an ANWB store before you leave.

facts.title: Plugs: type A/B, 100 V
facts.body: Mains is 100 V (50 Hz east, 60 Hz west) with flat two-pin type A sockets (some B). Most phone and laptop chargers handle 100–240 V; check hair dryers and the like.

facts.title: Earthquake alert apps
facts.body: The Dutch advice names Yurekuru Call, Japan Shelter Guide, Safetytips, NHK World-Japan and Tokyo Minato City.
